original_summary: Knaves is a three-player trick-taking game with a 52-card deck and a trump suit set by a turned-up card. Each trick taken scores +1, and capturing the four Jacks costs -1, -2, -3 or -4 points. The first player to reach 20 points over several hands wins.

review.evidence: No simple policy is safe. Always playing your highest card wins tricks but also collects the Jacks that others discard, and a Jack trick can be worth -3 overall. Always playing your lowest card gives up tricks. Every card choice changes who takes which trick and who eats which Jack. One seat imbalance exists: the rules never rotate the deal or the first lead, so eldest always leads first.

Card play, counting and Jack-dumping are real skills. But with 17-card hands, a hand rich in trumps and aces takes many tricks almost regardless of play, and nothing makes up for a weak deal. Over a few hands to 20, the deal often decides the winner.
There is a lot to improve at: counting trumps, inferring voids from discards, timing when to win or lose a trick, and steering Jacks to the leader. A weak player still takes some tricks and scores.
Hands are hidden. Every play leaks information (failing to follow reveals a void), and planning which tricks to win or duck over a whole hand takes inference and opponent modelling.
The trick winner follows from suit and rank. Scores are trick counts minus fixed Jack penalties, and the target is a plain number.

Hidden hands and sequential plays are supported. But one hand is 17 tricks, and reaching 20 points can take three or more hands, so 50+ rounds against a 40-round limit. A 52-card deck is also a lot of state to track. 'First to 20' can be reached by two players in the same hand, with no tie rule.

problems: Length: 17 tricks per hand, played to 20 points, exceeds the 40-round limit and has an unpredictable length.
Lottery: hand strength largely decides trick count, and nothing in the scoring rewards playing a weak hand well, so the deal often decides the winner.
Seat edge: the rules never rotate the deal or the first lead.
The winner rule is incomplete: two players can pass 20 in the same hand, and there is no tie rule.
Scale: a 52-card deck with 17-card hands is far more state than needed to keep the game's decisions.

changes.what: Shrink the deck to 20 cards (A, K, Q, J, 10 in each suit). Deal 6 cards to each player. Turn the 19th card up for trump and leave the 20th face down, out of play.
changes.why: This keeps the original's structure of three equal hands, one turned-up trump card and leftover cards out of play, at a size the engine can track. Each hand becomes 6 tricks.
changes.fixes: Scale: a 52-card deck with 17-card hands is far more state than needed to keep the game's decisions.

changes.what: Play exactly 6 hands (36 tricks, one trick per round). The highest total wins, and a tie for highest is a draw.
changes.why: This gives a fixed length inside 40 rounds and a complete winner rule. Endgame unraveling does not apply, because this is not a cooperation game.
changes.fixes: Length: 17 tricks per hand, played to 20 points, exceeds the 40-round limit and has an unpredictable length.

changes.what: Rotate the dealer every hand. The player left of the dealer (eldest) leads the first trick. Over 6 hands, each player is dealer twice and eldest twice.
changes.why: This removes any built-in seat advantage.
changes.fixes: Seat edge: the rules never rotate the deal or the first lead.

changes.what: Add a secret simultaneous bid at the start of each hand. Each player predicts how many tricks they will take (0 to 6). Bids are revealed before the first lead, and an exact bid earns +4.
changes.why: A weak hand can now score well by bidding low and ducking accurately, so the deal changes what to do rather than who wins. Revealed bids give opponents a target to read and disrupt: they can force tricks on a player who bid low, or refuse tricks to one who bid high.
changes.fixes: Lottery: hand strength largely decides trick count, and nothing in the scoring rewards playing a weak hand well, so the deal often decides the winner.

changes.what: Make each trick worth 2 points and keep the Jack penalties unchanged (spades -1, clubs -2, diamonds -3, hearts -4).
changes.why: With only 6 tricks per hand, worth 1 each, the -10 of Jack penalties would swamp trick-taking. At 2 points per trick (12 per hand), tricks and Jacks keep roughly the original balance against each other.
changes.fixes: Lottery: hand strength largely decides trick count, and nothing in the scoring rewards playing a weak hand well, so the deal often decides the winner.

keeps: Three players, a trick-taking game with must-follow-suit and a trump suit set by a turned-up card
A leftover card out of play, as in the original's 52nd card
Tricks score points; the four Jacks carry graded penalties of -1, -2, -3 and -4 by suit
The central tension of Knaves: wanting tricks while dodging, and dumping, the expensive Jacks

recommendation.reason: The game's decisions (follow suit, trump, Jack-dumping, inference from discards) fit the engine once the deck and hand length are cut down. An exact-bid bonus turns deal luck into a planning problem.

variation.name: Knaves' Wager
variation.summary: A short three-player Knaves played with a 20-card deck over 6 hands of 6 tricks. Players take tricks, avoid the Jacks and secretly predict their trick count each hand for a bonus.
variation.rules:
PLAYERS AND DECK. 3 players sit in a fixed order. The deck has 20 cards: A, K, Q, J, 10 in each of spades, clubs, diamonds and hearts. Within a suit, cards rank A (high), K, Q, J, 10 (low).

HANDS AND ROUNDS. The game is 6 hands of 6 tricks each, 36 rounds in all. Each round is one trick. The dealer for hand 1 is player 1. The dealer moves one seat to the left each hand, so each player deals twice. The player to the dealer's left is eldest for that hand.

DEAL (first round of each hand). Shuffle all 20 cards. Deal 6 cards privately to each player; a hand is seen only by its owner. Turn the 19th card face up: its suit is trump for this hand, and the card itself is out of play. The 20th card stays face down and out of play, and is never revealed during the hand.

BID (first round of each hand, after the deal). All players at the same moment secretly choose a whole number from 0 to 6: the number of tricks they predict they will take this hand. All three bids are then revealed to everyone.

TRICK PLAY (every round). The leader plays any card from their hand face up. The eldest leads the first trick of a hand; afterwards, the winner of the previous trick leads. Then the next player to the left plays, then the third. Each must play a card of the led suit if they have one. If they have none, they may play any card, including a trump. The trick is won by the highest trump in it. If it holds no trump, the highest card of the led suit wins. All plays are visible to everyone as they are made.

TRICK SCORING. The trick winner adds 2 to their hand score. They also take penalties for any Jacks in the trick: Jack of spades -1, Jack of clubs -2, Jack of diamonds -3, Jack of hearts -4. The trick's cards, its winner and the running trick counts are announced.

END OF HAND (after the 6th trick). Any player whose tricks taken equal their bid adds 4 to their hand score. Each player's hand score (2 per trick, minus Jack penalties, plus any bid bonus) is added to their total and announced. Hand scores reset to 0, and the dealer rotates.

END OF GAME. After the 6th hand (round 36), the game ends.
variation.objective: After 6 hands, the player with the highest total wins. If two or three players tie for the highest total, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Players must judge their hand to bid, then steer the trick count towards that bid while dumping Jacks on rivals and avoiding taking them. Because bids are public, opponents can see who needs or must avoid tricks and act against them: force a trick on a low bidder, or ruff a high bidder's ace. A weak deal can still win through an accurate low bid and careful ducking, so the deal decides what to do more than who wins. The single unseen card keeps card-counting slightly uncertain. Thoughtless policies lose: always-highest overshoots its bid and collects Jacks, always-lowest misses tricks and often its bid, and random play does both. Talk is left out. Its only real conflict use is two players agreeing to gang up on the leader, which turns the result into kingmaking rather than card reasoning. Free talk could also let players reveal hands. The plays themselves already carry the signals worth reading.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFF ARITHMETIC PER HAND: 6 tricks x 2 = 12 trick points in total. The four Jacks carry -10 in penalties, but on average 18 of the 20 cards are in play, so about -9 is assessed. That leaves about +3 net from tricks, roughly +1 per player per hand. The exact-bid bonus is +4. Bidding accuracy therefore matters more than raw trick count, and Jack-dumping (a void player discards a Jack onto an opponent's trick) is a real tactic.

KEY DECISION TABLE (one player's hand score, given tricks won t and Jack penalty p in those tricks):
- bid = t: 2t - p + 4
- bid != t: 2t - p
- Examples: bid 0, made: 4. Bid 2, made, no Jacks: 8. Bid 2, made, J-hearts taken: 4. Bid 2, took 3 with J-diamonds: 3.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (highest 6-hand total wins):
(a) Always bid 0 and play the lowest legal card. Ducking is not controllable: a hand holding a trump Ace, or forced to follow suit with high cards, must win tricks. With 6 of 20 cards, P(0 tricks) is well under 1/2, so the expected score is about 4 x P(make) < 2 per hand. Sensible players bid their honest estimate. They get about +1 from tricks plus 4 x P(make) with higher accuracy, because they control the trick count in both directions. Policy (a) loses most games against sensible play. Against random bidders it sometimes wins, but not almost always.
(b) Always bid 6. This is made only with a near-perfect hand, so the bonus is almost never earned. It loses to sensible play.
(c) Always play the highest card. This takes Jack-laden tricks and makes bids only by accident. It loses.
(d) Always bid the first or last option (0 or 6) is the same as (a) or (b).
No bid and no card is strictly better whatever the opponents do. The best bid depends on the hand, on trump and on the opponents' bids and play.

SEAT EDGE: the dealer rotates, so each player deals twice and is eldest twice over 6 hands. The leading advantage is shared equally. Bids are simultaneous, so there is no information edge from bid order.

WINNABILITY: totals are integers over a wide range, so ties (draws) are rare. All three players can realistically win. There is no cooperation or dilemma framing to mislabel.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: the deck (20 cards), ranks, deal (6/6/6, 19th card face-up for trump and out of play, 20th hidden), simultaneous bid 0-6, follow-suit rule, trick winner (highest trump, else highest card of the led suit), leader rule, scoring and draw rule are all specified. All cards are distinct, so no trick can tie. Six cards each over six tricks means hands empty exactly at hand end. A turned-up Jack is out of play and never scored, which is consistent with 'trick's cards'.

FINITE: exactly 36 rounds.

ARITHMETIC DECISION: the winner is the highest total, and the totals are kept by the game.

LIMITS:
- Choices per round: round 1 of a hand has 1 simultaneous bid plus 3 sequential card plays = 4 (limit 4). Other rounds have 3.
- Steps: 12 is within 20. Trick resolution is a calc on suit/rank encodings. Follow-suit legality is a single rule check the referee may rule on. A conditional bid bonus uses a 'when' or 'if' on a single step, which is allowed.
- Attributes: per player bid, tricks, hand score and total = 12, plus trump suit and led suit = 14 (limit 20). Leader and dealer can be derived or are within slack.
- Hidden elements: private hands and the face-down 20th card = 2 (limit 3).
- Random draws: one shuffle in a hand's first round, 0 otherwise (limit 1).
- Rounds: 36 (limit 40).
No board, clock, trading or binding agreements are needed. Bids use a simultaneous poll, as required.

TALK: none is used. This is sensible here. Public bids already supply the information players need to read each other, and play is a visible, sequential trick contest. Free talk would mostly add cheap, unenforceable bluff, and players are not reduced to blind guessing without it.

The repeated-cooperation concern does not apply: this is not a dilemma game.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE: the deal strongly shapes how many tricks a hand can take. However, the scoring rewards accurate prediction (+4) more than strength (about +1 net per hand from tricks). A weak hand that bids 0 or 1 accurately scores comparably to a strong hand. Over 6 hands with rotating lead, single-deal luck is averaged. I estimate chance decides roughly 30-40% of outcomes between equal players, and much less between a good and a poor player.

INFERENCE AVAILABLE:
- Card counting is very tractable: only 20 cards, with 1 visible out and 1 hidden out.
- Opponents' public bids reveal their hand strength and intended trick counts.
- Voids are revealed by failures to follow suit.
- Jack location (who still holds J-hearts).

WAYS TO ACT ON IT:
- Bid calibration.
- Ducking or overtaking to hit your own bid.
- Forcing an unwanted trick onto an opponent who bid low, or starving one who bid high.
- Dumping Jacks onto rivals' tricks.

ALL-GOOD-PLAY OUTCOME: if all three play well, the winner comes from accumulated small edges in bid accuracy, Jack placement and sabotage over 36 tricks, not from a single hidden type or deal. Good play can overcome a bad deal, because a low accurate bid still earns +4. A reasoning player is clearly favoured.
